challenges.name: Who pays, and dispute proof
challenges.one: Visa puts enrolled agents' purchases on the cardholder, Link on the user. Disputes still use human reason codes.
challenges.arch: Name the loss holder per route before launch. Write evidence before payment: mandate, cart served, agent id and key snapshot, kept for the rail's dispute window.
challenges.pain: If the agent buys the wrong thing, I cannot tell who pays me back.
challenges.working: Visa agentic rules, Amex promised cover, UK Treasury, FCA, Cloudflare coalition.
challenges.research: A valid mandate signature does not prove what the user intended.

challenges.name: Trust to press pay
challenges.one: Only 23 to 28 percent of US shoppers are comfortable letting an agent pay.
challenges.arch: Keep a human approval above a threshold, show cart and merchant before pay, and make disputes one tap. 32 percent accept agent choice with final approval.
challenges.pain: I will let it choose, but I want to approve before it pays.
challenges.working: Visa and Mastercard agent programs, Amex promised cover, six bank principles.
challenges.research: Users with weaker agents got worse deals and did not notice.

challenges.name: Telling good agents from bad
challenges.one: Merchants cannot tell a trusted agent from a bad bot, and fraud models tuned to humans misread both.
challenges.arch: Tier 2 for a signature plus mandate, or registered agent, agentic token and passkey. Score unsigned browsers as normal card sales. Send the agent signal at authorization.
challenges.pain: We cannot tell good agents from bad bots, so we block both and lose sales.
challenges.working: Visa and Mastercard Web Bot Auth, Cloudflare verified bots, Mastercard agent score.
challenges.research: Stored cards hide the agent from the issuer's risk controls.

challenges.name: Platforms shut agents out
challenges.one: Amazon bars 99 named AI agents and crawlers, and calls its own agent primary.
challenges.arch: Use sanctioned routes such as UCP endpoints, feeds and MCP servers, identify the agent, and honour merchant access files. Merchants should publish an agent access policy.
challenges.pain: The biggest store shuts my agent out, so it cannot shop where I shop.
challenges.working: Ninth Circuit Comet ruling, a Shopify storefront routing agents to UCP, network key directories.
challenges.research: Attackers already use open source agent frameworks to breach retailers and other companies.

challenges.name: Mandates outlive user intent
challenges.one: Spend limits, product scope and revocation are weakly expressed, so an agent's authority can outlast the user's wish.
challenges.arch: The agent platform or network enforces limits and expiry. The merchant checks the cart against the authority record, enforces consume once and logs revocations.
challenges.pain: I switched the agent off, and now I have to prove it.
challenges.working: AP2 open and closed mandates, Mastercard Verifiable Intent, Visa consumer instructions.
challenges.research: In simulation, consume once mandates bound to context stopped replay at 3.8 ms.

challenges.name: Wrong or steered purchases
challenges.one: Agents still buy the wrong thing, hidden prompts steer them, and LLM pitches steer users.
challenges.arch: Treat merchant content as untrusted, isolate it from cart building, check the cart against the mandate before pay, and record what the agent saw and its model version.
challenges.pain: My agent bought something I did not want, and I could not tell why.
challenges.working: Visa benchmark, PCAT defence research, x402 SDK spend caps, AP2 cart mandates.
challenges.research: Visa benchmark: 54 percent of failed runs still ended in a purchase decision.

challenges.name: Banks refuse agent access
challenges.one: Citi, Bank of America and JPMorgan keep outside agents from moving money, and banks shift risk to customers.
challenges.arch: Never ask for bank logins. Use network tokens or read only connectors, and record revocation with a timestamp the user can show. Wells Fargo requires proof from 2026-11-24.
challenges.pain: My bank says sharing my login with an agent makes me answer for it.
challenges.working: Plaid read only connectors, network agent tokens, Bank of America and Wells Fargo terms.
challenges.research: Reg E treats transfers by someone handed the access device as authorized until notice.

challenges.name: Rules assume a human
challenges.one: Payment rules expect a person to approve each payment, which slows delegated agent payments on regulated rails.
challenges.arch: Authenticate at delegation where rules allow, then step up per country: EU SCA when an agent pays or sets a merchant initiated mandate, two factors in India.
challenges.pain: We cannot offer delegated payments because the rules expect a human to approve each one.
challenges.working: HM Treasury consultation, FCA AI Live Testing, MAS 2027 consultation, NPCI reported agent protocol.
challenges.research: SCA elements assume human interaction, and PISP status for agents is open.

challenges.name: Protocol churn and integration cost
challenges.one: Specs break between releases, and every new agent surface asks merchants and payment providers to rebuild.
challenges.arch: Wait with readiness until your agent share passes our proposed 3% trigger for two months running. Then budget each adapter per breaking release, or let the PSP absorb it.
challenges.pain: Specs change under us, and every new agent surface asks us to rebuild.
challenges.working: Visa Intelligent Commerce Connect, Adyen Agentic, UCP technical councils.
challenges.research: A formal analysis found 40 undocumented consistency findings across four agent payment protocols.

challenges.name: Losing the customer and margin
challenges.one: Agent platforms may own the customer, charge up to 4 percent, and hide which sales they sent.
challenges.arch: Tag every agent order with the platform id, offer account linking so the customer record stays yours, and track each platform's fee per surface.
challenges.pain: The agent owns my customer, takes a cut, and I cannot see which sales it sent.
challenges.working: UCP identity linking, Personal Agent Protocol, Adobe referral measurement.
challenges.research: Only 37 percent of leaders have a plan to keep the direct relationship.

routes.name: Visa card, enrolled agent
routes.one: Visa's rules make the cardholder answer for an enrolled agent, as if they paid themselves.
routes.arch: Rule 4.1.23.10, added 2026-04. No agent dispute condition, so disputes run on reason codes built for human buyers.
routes.open: Will a signed mandate count as dispute evidence?

routes.name: Mastercard card
routes.one: No rule text found. Its guide says normal chargeback rights apply.
routes.arch: Developer guide: standard fraud, chargeback and dispute processes apply, and agents take on consumer checks. Rules PDF unread.
routes.open: Will Mastercard publish a rule like Visa's?

routes.name: Stripe Link agent wallet
routes.one: The user pays for every agent purchase, even a different item from the one shown.
routes.arch: Link agent wallet FAQ. Purchase Protections are US only, discretionary and silent on agents.
routes.open: How do these terms sit with card chargeback rights?

routes.name: Amex card
routes.one: Agent Purchase Protection is promised for registered agents, not yet live.
routes.arch: Cover for registered agents with authenticated intent. Announced, no live integrations found.
routes.open: When does the cover go live, and for whom?

routes.name: Card dispute, not fraud
routes.one: The merchant carries a wrong item dispute by default, unless it wins.
routes.arch: Non fraud card disputes default to the merchant. No network has an agent reason code yet.
routes.open: Will networks add an agent reason code?

routes.name: US bank login shared
routes.one: One law firm reads US rules as putting it on the customer until they revoke access.
routes.arch: Goodwin on Reg E 1005.2(m): access given to an agent counts as authorised until the bank is told, unless the bank broke its own procedure.
routes.open: Does an AI provider count as a person given the access device?

routes.name: UK online payment
routes.one: For an unauthorised online payment the payer carries no loss. This is our reading.
routes.arch: PSRs 2017 reg 77(4)(c) and (d), and 77(6) for a payee side that skipped strong checks. Our reading, not a regulator view.
routes.open: Is a payment inside the user's mandate authorised?

routes.name: Stablecoin payment
routes.one: Final on chain. The payer has no way back unless the seller refunds.
routes.arch: x402 defines no refund or dispute process. Refunds happen only by the seller's agreement.
routes.open: Who offers buyer recourse on final rails?

routes.name: Agent checked at the CDN
routes.one: Cloudflare's coalition says the site pays when a user disputes an agent purchase.
routes.arch: Trusted Agent Delegation post, 2026-11-05. Identity tiers only, no named members and no rule text.
routes.open: Will any site sign up to carry that loss?

places.name: United States
places.one: No agent law. The consumer regulator is silent, and a Fed governor asked who pays.
places.arch: No CFPB statement found by 2026-11-15. Card network rules lead, with Visa's 4.1.23.10 the only agent text.
places.next: Card networks may write the first rule

places.name: European Union
places.one: New payment law is near final but does not mention agents.
places.arch: PSR final vote planned 2026-12-14, applying about late 2028. An industry council works on agent refunds for local payment methods.

places.name: United Kingdom
places.one: Treasury asked about agent liability, and the FCA plans a trust framework.
places.arch: Treasury Question 15 closed 2026-10-06 with no response yet. Regulators say existing law applies to personal agents.

places.name: India
places.one: Two factor checks on every digital payment, with no agent text.
places.arch: RBI Authentication Directions apply from 2026-04-01. A reported agent protocol on UPI has no confirmed launch.
places.next: Launch of an agent protocol on UPI

places.name: Singapore
places.one: AI risk rules apply from 2027-10, and agent guidance goes to consultation in 2027.
places.arch: MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines issued 2026-10-07. Firms stay responsible for third party AI.

redteam.one: Our main bet held in every scenario, so nothing could prove it wrong.
redteam.arch: The thesis had no exit test, and its build trigger could not be measured.
redteam.change: Added a wait option and a trigger you can measure.

redteam.one: Building around the signed mandate put the least settled part in the core.
redteam.arch: Mandate formats still change, so a mandate centred core would churn with every spec.
redteam.change: The core keeps a thin record of five fields plus the signed original.

redteam.one: No wait option, and no world where agents suggest and people pay.
redteam.arch: The evidence points to agents that refer while people still pay, and the options ignored it.
redteam.change: Added wait with readiness, and an agents refer, people pay scenario.

redteam.one: A merchant gateway cannot cap an agent's spend at other merchants.
redteam.arch: Buyer side controls such as cross merchant spend caps sit outside the merchant's reach.
redteam.change: Spend caps across merchants move to the buyer side and the network.

redteam.one: The ranking rewarded writing specs and ignored who controls the token.
redteam.arch: Spec authorship was over weighted against control of the credential layer.
redteam.change: Players rescored with a token layer measure.

redteam.one: Virtual cards and agent browsers on stored cards were missing.
redteam.arch: Two live patterns were absent from the comparison and the decision tree.
redteam.change: Added both, with stored cards as the one to avoid.

redteam.one: Key build choices were missing, such as agent flags at authorization.
redteam.arch: Missing: agent signal in authorization, CIT and MIT, account linking, fees and amount drift.
redteam.change: Three new parameters joined the build list.

redteam.one: Two scenarios were already happening together, and none had a dated test.
redteam.arch: Scenarios overlapped and lacked falsifiable, dated kill tests.
redteam.change: Each scenario now has a dated kill test.

redteam.one: Building to the token moves lock in to the network and the payment provider.
redteam.arch: Token portability depends on the token requestor, so lock in shifts rather than disappears.
redteam.change: Kept the bet, and added a contract question on who holds the token.

redteam.one: Scoring weights had no basis, and fraud and privacy had no say.
redteam.arch: Weights were unexplained, and fraud, customer ownership and privacy were unscored.
redteam.change: Liability became a gate, and weights got a stated basis.

redteam.one: The worked example compared layers as if they were rivals.
redteam.arch: It ranked options from different stack layers against each other.
redteam.change: Rebuilt the example to compare like with like.

redteam.one: A tier rule would have refused the consumer flows that are live today.
redteam.arch: The tier 2 rule blocked live consumer flows that cannot yet meet it.
redteam.change: Relaxed the tier rule for live consumer flows.

redteam.one: Too many parameter rows, mixing choices with context.
redteam.arch: 37 rows mixed design choices, context fields and evidence fields.
redteam.change: Kept the rows, tagged each one, and the page shows only the choices.

redteam.one: The challenge ranking hid two tiers and missed churn, attribution and fees.
redteam.arch: Ties hid a two tier ranking, and three pains were missing.
redteam.change: Merged two pairs and added churn and margin challenges.

redteam.one: Tempo was counted twice and may sit inside Stripe's orbit.
redteam.arch: MPP authorship counted for both Stripe and Tempo.
redteam.change: Tempo left the startup list.

redteam.one: Cloudflare's coalition launch was missed.
redteam.arch: A dated market move inside the window was not scored.
redteam.change: Scored as a move, since it names no members yet.

redteam.one: Some answers ended in flows nobody can build today.
redteam.arch: Several leaves pointed to flows with no shipped implementation.
redteam.change: Changed the tree endings to flows you can build.

redteam.one: Saying every payment can be defended overclaimed, and nobody owned privacy.
redteam.arch: ADR-4 overclaimed defensibility and gave the evidence store no privacy owner.
redteam.change: Softened the claim, and the evidence store got a privacy owner.

redteam.one: The speed target for agent checks has never been tested.
redteam.arch: The 300 ms p95 target has no production measurement behind it.
redteam.change: Marked as a target. Still open.

redteam.one: Small mismatches between sections.
redteam.arch: Internal slips across sections 1.3, 2.3 and 8.
redteam.change: Fixed across the doc.

decide.name: Tag agent orders
decide.one: Mark every order an agent placed, so you can see your own share.
decide.arch: Tag P28 on every order. Your agent completed share (V17) is what fires the build trigger in ADR-1.
decide.trigger: Without the tag, our proposed 3% trigger cannot fire.

decide.name: Name who pays
decide.one: Before launch, write down who carries a wrong agent purchase on each payment route.
decide.arch: Map each route to its loss holder and basis, network rule, terms or chargeback rights, before go live.
decide.trigger: Any agent order on a new route.

decide.name: Evidence before payment
decide.one: Save the purchase record before money moves, and keep it only while disputes can happen.
decide.arch: Write evidence before the PSP call, then append the result. Retention is the longest dispute window of the rail (V18).

decide.name: Trust tiers for agents
decide.one: Let agents browse freely, and ask for more proof before they pay.
decide.arch: Tier 0 browse, tier 1 cart, tier 2 pay. Tier 2 needs a signature plus mandate, or a registered agent, agentic token and passkey.

decide.name: Build to the token
decide.one: Keep your payment provider until agent orders pass our proposed trigger, then build.
decide.arch: Below the trigger, wait with readiness. Above it, canonical model plus adapters, or the PSP if it exports evidence.
decide.trigger: Our proposed 3% trigger for two months running.

decide.name: Pay per call apart
decide.one: Keep tiny machine payments on their own path, away from card checkout.
decide.arch: HTTP 402 calls settle through a facilitator. Budgets sit in the buyer's wallet, never as prepaid balances you hold.
